title: Retrieved and tool-returned content enters the model context with no provenance label a runtime can enforce
problem: I splice a fetched page, an issue thread or a retrieved document into the model's context, and from that point no component in my stack can say which tokens came from my operator and which came from a stranger.
symptom: The agent takes an action nobody asked for after reading external content, and the trace shows the instruction it obeyed sitting inline in tool output, formatted exactly like the operator's own prompt.
why_now: Serving APIs accept one flat token sequence. The system/user/assistant/tool roles are a conversational convention, not an enforced trust boundary, and tool results are appended as ordinary text. The defences that actually shipped through 2025 - delimiters, appended instructions to ignore adversarial content, and injection classifiers - all operate inside that same flat stream and are probabilistic, so there is still no field a runtime can read to decide whether a span is permitted to issue instructions.
existing: Delimiters and spotlighting: the attacker controls the content and can imitate or argue past the delimiter, and nothing enforces the boundary.
Security thought reinforcement, Google's shipped name for appending instructions to ignore adversarial ones: one probabilistic instruction competing with another inside the same stream.
Prompt-injection classifiers that filter untrusted content before it reaches the model: a detector with a false-negative rate, not a contract, and vendors report reduction rather than elimination.
Control-and-data-flow separation of the CaMeL kind does give enforceable provenance, but it requires re-expressing the agent as an interpreted program and it costs task utility.
A protocol-level fix is under discussion rather than shipped: MCP SEP-1913 proposes trust and sensitivity annotations with propagation rules, and it has been open and unmerged since November 2025.

evidence.title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
evidence.quote: We argue that LLM-Integrated Applications blur the line between data and instructions.
evidence.note: Venue confirmed out of band via the DBLP API (AISec@CCS 2023, pages 79-90, doi 10.1145/3605764.3623985), because dl.acm.org returned HTTP 403 to this agent. The paper states the data/instruction confusion as the root defect and adds that effective mitigations are lacking.

evidence.title: The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication
evidence.quote: LLMs are unable to reliably distinguish the importance of instructions based on where they came from. Everything eventually gets glued together into a sequence of tokens and fed to the model.
evidence.note: States the missing contract precisely: origin is not represented in the artifact the model consumes.

evidence.title: Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy
evidence.quote: This technique adds targeted security instructions surrounding the prompt content to remind the large language model (LLM) to perform the user-directed task and ignore any adversarial instructions that could be present in the content.
evidence.note: This is the mitigation Google actually shipped for Gemini in Workspace, and it is an instruction inside the same flat stream rather than a provenance label. The same post frames the whole layered strategy as raising attacker cost, not as elimination.

evidence.title: SEP-1913: Trust and Sensitivity Annotations
evidence.quote: Data from untrusted sources enters context without markers
evidence.note: SEP-1913 in the official MCP specification repository, opened 2025-11-27 by SamMorrowDrums with @dend cc'd as sponsor, author_association CONTRIBUTOR. Confirmed via the GitHub API on 2026-08-16 as state=open, merged=false, 41 issue comments and 31 review comments, last updated 2026-08-03. An unmerged proposal after eight months of discussion is direct evidence that the contract does not exist in the protocol today, from the tracker of the people who own it. The proposal names indirect prompt injection as its first motivation and lists declassification and cross-server annotation sharing as still-open questions.

build_hypothesis: A provenance-carrying context assembler: every span appended to a prompt is tagged with its origin and trust level at insertion time, the assembler refuses to emit a prompt in which a low-trust span is unfenced, and the tag survives into the trace so a reviewer can attribute the instruction the agent actually obeyed.

check.manual_question: Follow one span of externally fetched text from the tool that produced it to the token stream you send the model. Which component records that this span came from an untrusted origin, and which component would refuse to send it unfenced?
check.rationale: The gap is the absence of any provenance concept, so the signature is lexical: a codebase that both ingests external content and calls a model, yet nowhere names a trust level, taint or provenance for that content, has no contract to enforce - only a convention in prose. It over-reports for a project that achieves separation architecturally without the vocabulary (a separate process, a schema-only tool boundary), which is why the mitigation rule requires positive evidence and the manual question exists.
